name: Electron
summary: A desktop application framework that combines a privileged main process with Chromium renderer contexts, explicit IPC bridges, and utility processes for web-based user interfaces.

features.name: Main and renderer process boundary
features.description: Electron documents a main process that runs the application lifecycle and creates BrowserWindow instances, while each BrowserWindow runs page content in a renderer process. Renderer processes are Chromium web contexts and do not directly own the native application lifecycle.
benefits: Separates native window control from web content execution
Allows Chromium renderer isolation and independent page contexts
costs: Application behavior crosses asynchronous process boundaries
Window and renderer lifetimes must be coordinated explicitly

features.name: Preload capability bridge
features.description: A preload script runs before page loading and can expose a deliberately selected API to the renderer. Electron's tutorial recommends context isolation and exposing narrow functions rather than handing untrusted content the complete IPC module; sandboxed preload execution has a restricted environment.
benefits: Makes native capabilities explicit at the web/native boundary
Supports least-authority APIs for renderer code
costs: Every exposed method becomes a security and validation surface
Sandbox and context-isolation constraints limit available Node APIs

features.name: IPC channel model
features.description: Electron provides main-side ipcMain and renderer-side ipcRenderer APIs with send, invoke/handle, and event channels. The documented preload pattern converts these channels into application-specific functions, while the source implements native IPC dispatch at the renderer and browser boundaries.
benefits: Lets applications define a smaller protocol than the framework API
costs: Serialization, sender validation, and error propagation are application responsibilities
Channel names and payload contracts must remain compatible across processes

features.name: Utility process isolation
features.description: Electron exposes utilityProcess for starting Node.js environments in separate child processes and communicating with them through MessagePorts. The utility process API provides a separate lifecycle and failure boundary for work that should not run in the main or renderer process.
benefits: Moves selected Node workloads outside the main process
Provides an additional process boundary for fault containment
costs: Additional processes increase startup, memory, and supervision cost
Message passing replaces direct in-process calls

mathematical_views.question: How do main, renderer, preload, and utility process nodes connect through window ownership and IPC edges?
assumptions: Processes and execution contexts are explicit nodes
Window ownership and message channels are labeled edges
The graph abstracts Chromium scheduling and operating-system process details

mathematical_views.question: Which native operations can a renderer access after a preload bridge refines a broad framework API into application-specific functions?
assumptions: The exposed API is a subset of main-process handlers
IPC serialization and sender checks are part of the protocol boundary
Security equivalence is a hypothesis requiring review of each exposed method

mathematical_views.question: What transitions connect application startup, window creation, renderer failure, utility-process exit, and application shutdown?
assumptions: Renderer and utility processes can fail independently of the main process
The model abstracts platform-specific shutdown behavior

benefits: Native control and web content have separate failure and privilege domains
costs: Cross-process lifecycle coordination adds latency and state-management work

benefits: A narrow bridge can reduce renderer authority
costs: Bridge design and validation determine the effective security boundary

benefits: Explicit channels support decoupled process communication
costs: Protocol compatibility and serialization become application obligations

benefits: Selected workloads gain a separate process failure boundary
costs: Extra processes consume resources and require supervision
